record.narrative: The first registered set targets biologically interpretable oncogene-addiction and selective-loss-of-function/synthetic-lethal relationships among the CRISPR dependency scores. For most dependencies, more negative scores mean stronger dependency. Negative-direction claims therefore predict exposed-minus-comparator raw differences below zero. Specifically, braf_v600e-positive lines are hypothesized to depend more on BRAF; kras_mutation-positive lines are hypothesized to depend more on KRAS and plausibly more on RIT1 as a related RAS-pathway node; egfr_amplification and erbb2_amplification are hypothesized to strengthen EGFR, ERBB2, and related signaling/trafficking dependencies. TP53 loss is expected to weaken MDM2 and RPL11 dependencies, so the expected raw difference is positive and the claim direction is +1. SMARCA4 loss is expected to strengthen SMARCA2 dependency, KEAP1 loss is expected to strengthen NFE2L2/NRF2 dependency, and MSI-high status is expected to strengthen WRN dependency. MYC amplification is used to probe transcriptional dependencies POLR2A, DHX9, and USP7; CDKN2A loss is used to probe mitotic dependency KIF18A. EGFR amplification is also tested for TMED10 trafficking/secretory dependence, and ERBB2 amplification for STAT3 dependence. These are discovery comparisons within supplied lung-lineage cell lines only; they are associations, not causal or generalizable claims. Later analyses should inspect whether signed estimates are both statistically credible (95% intervals away from zero and cell counts adequate) and clinically meaningful under the relative difference threshold, noting that a 10% difference corresponds to roughly 0.02-0.05 for many dependencies with means near -0.25, while broader outcomes such as SMARCA2, STAT3, WRN, NFE2L2, USP7, and MDM2 may require context-specific effect-size assessment.

I selected the first 12 registered hypotheses because they cover the strongest high-prior biological relationships and span all four planned primary axes: oncogene addiction for BRAF, KRAS, EGFR, and ERBB2; TP53-MDM2 attenuation; synthetic lethal chromatin dependency for SMARCA4/SMARCA2; KEAP1-NFE2L2 oxidative-stress dependency; MSI-WRN dependency; MYC-amplification transcriptional dependencies; and KRAS-associated RAS-pathway/RIT1 dependency. Each exposure is binary with expected cell counts above the required minimum of 20 observations per cell based on dataset frequencies, including rarer exposures such as braf_v600e, egfr_amplification, erbb2_amplification, and msi_high. These analyses are discovery associations within the supplied lung-lineage dataset; no accept/reject assessment is made now because no numerical evidence is present yet.

All estimates are already signed to the registered hypothesis direction, so a positive signed estimate supports a negative-direction dependency claim (raw exposed-minus-comparator more negative) and a negative signed estimate opposes it. H6, SMARCA4 loss versus dependency_SMARCA2, is an unambiguous accepted association in this dataset: signed mean_difference +0.784, 95% CI +0.765 to +0.803, n 412 vs 1588. This is both far outside zero and enormous relative to the SMARCA2 outcome distribution, supporting the synthetic-lethal prediction within the supplied data only. H8, MSI-high versus dependency_WRN, is likewise accepted: signed estimate +0.790, CI +0.760 to +0.819, n 130 vs 1870, indicating much stronger WRN dependency in MSI-high lines in this dataset. H7, KEAP1 loss versus dependency_NFE2L2, strongly rejects the registered negative-direction hypothesis. Its signed estimate is -0.796 with CI -0.816 to -0.776; for direction -1 this corresponds to a positive raw exposed-minus-comparator difference, meaning KEAP1-loss lines have weaker rather than stronger NFE2L2 dependency. I rejected the original claim and proposed a reversed-direction claim to characterize this opposite association.

Most other claims are null or underpowered. H1 was rejected because the signed estimate was negative/opposite and the most favorable upper signed value was only +0.012, well below a likely 10% relative threshold for dependency_BRAF. H10-H12 were rejected because favorable upper bounds were small relative to their outcome scales and CIs included substantial opposite values; the point estimates were near zero. H2, H4, H5, and H9 remain unresolved because their intervals cross zero while allowing clinically meaningful positive signed differences in some cases. H3 is the most scientifically useful borderline result: EGFR amplification versus dependency_EGFR has signed estimate +0.0252, close to 10% relative to the outcome scale, but CI lower bound is -0.00025, so it is not credible without validation. I requested validation for H3. Multiple-comparison risk is low for H6-H8 given how far intervals exclude zero, but H3 remains unresolved because it is near zero and was part of a 12-test discovery family.

Because critical reviewers must consider technical confounding, I registered follow-up comparisons restricted to the dominant Avana CRISPR library and, for H6, to higher screen quality (screen_roc_auc >= 0.95). These do not change the accepted associations unless the effect fails, but they probe whether the huge H6 and H8 effects could partly reflect screen-platform or quality differences. I also registered a research-marker null-style check for dependency_SMARCA2 to detect latent association structure. All conclusions remain dataset-specific associations, not causal or generalizable claims.

The validation result for H3, EGFR amplification versus dependency_EGFR, does not support the original positive signed claim. The discovery estimate was only marginally favorable (+0.0252; CI approximately -0.0003 to +0.0507), and the independent validation estimate is opposite in sign (-0.0060) with an interval crossing zero and including clinically meaningful positive and negative values (-0.0497 to +0.0377). Because the independent interval still permits a meaningful positive effect, I do not treat this as definitive evidence against the association; however, the inconsistent and non-confirmatory validation evidence means H3 should not be accepted. I therefore assess H3 as unresolved and close the overall H3 investigation to prevent additional allocation to a low-confidence main effect unless a subgroup or refinement emerges separately.

I reassess H17 and accept it. H17 reverses the original KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 hypothesis: the signed estimate is +0.796 (CI +0.776 to +0.816) with n = 393 versus 1607. Since H17 has direction +1, this corresponds to a raw exposed-minus-comparator difference above zero, meaning KEAP1-loss lines have weaker, not stronger, NFE2L2 dependency in the supplied dataset. This is a very strong dataset-specific association, though unexpected relative to the usual KEAP1/NFE2L2 synthetic-lethal intuition. It should not be interpreted as causal or generalizable, and it deserves technical robustness checks because the outcome mean is near zero and the direction is opposite to the prior.

H6 and H8 remain the strongest accepted findings: SMARCA4 loss is associated with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, and MSI-high status is associated with much stronger WRN dependency. I propose quality-restricted and platform-restricted versions of these accepted findings, plus subtype-interaction analyses, to determine whether they persist across CRISPR screen quality and lineage subtype. I also register constructed research-marker null-style checks to probe whether latent marker effects contribute to the observed large dependency associations. The immediate priority is robustness of H6, H8, and especially H17, rather than pursuing H3 further.

The next round should separate robust accepted dataset associations from technical or biologic modifiers. For dependency_SMARCA2, dependency_WRN, and dependency_NFE2L2, the accepted effects are very large in the full lung-lineage dataset, but critical reviewers should still ask whether they persist in high-Cas9 screens, because Cas9 activity is an orthogonal screen-quality variable not covered by the Avana-library or screen_roc_auc restrictions. These are robustness tests, not new biology claims. I also registered modifier interactions: ARID1A loss may alter SMARCA2 dependency in SMARCA4-mutant backgrounds, and TP53 loss may alter the unexpectedly weaker NFE2L2 dependency associated with KEAP1 loss. For interactions, positive signed estimates indicate a stronger accepted-direction effect in the subgroup relative to its complement; I kept anticipated directions uncertain where no firm prior exists.

I added focused subgroup/broad biological follow-ups. EGFR amplification had an unresolved main effect with inconsistent validation, so testing EGFR amplification specifically in adenocarcinoma could reveal a subtype-specific effect rather than continuing the closed overall claim. I also registered biologically motivated predictor hypotheses for outcomes with unexplored or incomplete coverage: MYC amplification may strengthen ribosome-biogenesis-associated RPL11 dependency; PIK3CA mutation may strengthen STAT3 dependency through growth-pathway signaling; RB1 loss may strengthen KIF18A dependency because RB1 loss is associated with increased cell-cycle/mitotic pressure. All new negative-direction dependency claims expect stronger dependency, i.e. raw exposed-minus-comparator scores below zero, which will be returned as positive signed estimates. The 10% relative threshold is context dependent: outcomes centered near -0.25 to -0.28 correspond roughly to 0.025-0.028 absolute difference, while the accepted huge effects around 0.8 are far beyond any reasonable clinical threshold. All conclusions remain associations in this supplied dataset, not causal claims or generalized predictions.

No new evidence is available yet, so I do not change any claim assessments. I selected 12 registered comparisons to test now. First, I tested robustness of the three very large accepted associations under two technically relevant restrictions: the dominant Avana CRISPR library and higher screen quality (screen_roc_auc >= 0.95). For dependency_SMARCA2, dependency_WRN, and dependency_NFE2L2, these tests are important because an effect of magnitude near 0.8 would be scientifically meaningful only if it persists when excluding library or low-quality-screen artifacts. For signed negative-direction claims, persistence should appear as positive signed estimates near the original magnitude; for signed positive H17, persistence should remain large and positive. Second, I selected two mechanistically motivated interactions: ARID1A loss modifying SMARCA4-loss-associated SMARCA2 dependency, and TP53 loss modifying the KEAP1-loss-associated NFE2L2 dependency. Positive signed interaction estimates would indicate a stronger claim-direction effect within the named subgroup than in the complement, while negative estimates would indicate attenuation or heterogeneity. Third, I tested several high-prior unexplored biology claims: CDKN2A loss with KIF18A dependency, ERBB2 amplification with STAT3 dependency, MYC amplification with RPL11 dependency, and RB1 loss with KIF18A dependency. These add diversity beyond the currently accepted axes while remaining biologically plausible. All cell-count expectations are adequate for the binary exposures/subgroups selected, although interaction cell counts should still be checked diagnostically. Clinical significance will be judged contextually: for outcomes near -0.25, a 10% relative difference corresponds roughly to 0.025-0.030 absolute; for the already accepted broad outcomes, effects around 0.8 are far beyond any plausible threshold. These are discovery associations in the supplied lung-lineage dataset only, not causal or generalizable claims.

The new restricted analyses strongly support the robustness of the three major dataset associations already accepted. For dependency_SMARCA2, restricting to the dominant Avana library gives signed estimate +0.781 (95% CI +0.760 to +0.802; n 351 vs 1414), and restricting to higher screen quality (screen_roc_auc >= 0.95) gives +0.790 (+0.765 to +0.816; n 243 vs 918). For dependency_WRN, Avana restriction gives +0.794 (+0.764 to +0.825; n 120 vs 1645), and high screen quality gives +0.795 (+0.758 to +0.832; n 85 vs 1076). For dependency_NFE2L2, Avana restriction gives +0.796 (+0.774 to +0.818; n 353 vs 1412), and high screen quality gives +0.790 (+0.763 to +0.816; n 235 vs 926). These are not independent external confirmations, but they are same-dataset robustness checks: the huge signed effects remain essentially unchanged when dominant library or lower screen quality is excluded. I accept them as completed robustness checks and close these technical robustness investigations, while leaving the broader accepted claims active because other modifiers and null controls remain to be assessed.

The newly tested small-effect hypotheses mostly support nulls or inconclusive effects. H13, CDKN2A loss versus dependency_KIF18A, has signed estimate -0.0133 (CI -0.0332 to +0.0065); the entire signed interval is below the approximately 0.025-0.026 absolute threshold corresponding to a 10% relative difference for KIF18A-scale outcomes. It is therefore rejected and closed. H36, MYC amplification versus dependency_RPL11, has signed estimate -0.0125 (CI -0.0339 to +0.0090), also far below clinical significance and opposite in sign, so it is rejected and closed. H38, RB1 loss versus dependency_KIF18A, has point estimate +0.0082 (CI -0.0193 to +0.0357); it is not credible because the point is near null and the interval crosses both null and meaningful positive values, so I leave it unresolved and deferred rather than continue to prioritize it now.

H15, ERBB2 amplification versus dependency_STAT3, is the most useful borderline new result. Its signed estimate is +0.0222 (CI -0.0147 to +0.0592; n 162 vs 1838). This is near the 10% relative threshold for dependency_STAT3 but imprecise. Because H15 is biologically plausible, new, and eligible, I request independent validation for H15. Validation is preferable to spending another discovery test on this borderline effect because it could determine whether the result is a confirmatory dataset association or another low-confidence null.

The interaction analyses are inconclusive. H33, ARID1A loss modifying the SMARCA4-loss effect on dependency_SMARCA2, has positive signed interaction +0.0373 (CI -0.0148 to +0.0894). This suggests a stronger SMARCA4-loss association in ARID1A-positive lines, but the small ARID1A-positive SMARCA4-loss cell (n=76) gives wide uncertainty, and the point is near/below a 10% relative difference relative to SMARCA2 outcome scale. I keep it active and register a refinement that estimates the SMARCA4-loss effect directly within ARID1A-positive lines. H34, TP53 loss modifying the KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 association, is +0.0176 (CI -0.0340 to +0.0693); this is unresolved but low priority and deferred.

I also registered subgroup refinements for KRAS and ERBB2 in adenocarcinoma. These are reasonable because oncogene addiction may be subtype-specific and the main effects were unresolved, but they are follow-up hypotheses rather than current accepted claims. All conclusions remain associations in the supplied lung-lineage CRISPR dataset and are not causal or generalized.

The independent validation for H15, ERBB2 amplification versus dependency_STAT3, gives signed mean_difference +0.0243 with independent interval -0.0291 to +0.0776. This is very close to the discovery signed estimate +0.0222 and is not opposite in sign, unlike the H3 EGFR validation pattern. That consistency argues against treating the original discovery estimate as a one-sided fluke. However, the validation interval is wide because the independent validation comparison uses a stricter alpha, it crosses zero, and the lower tail includes a clinically relevant opposite-direction difference. Moreover, the point estimate itself is below the task's 10% relative-effect threshold for an outcome with mean around -0.28: a 10% difference is roughly 0.028 absolute, whereas the validation point is about 0.024 and the discovery point about 0.022. The data therefore support a suggestive small positive association between ERBB2 amplification and stronger STAT3 dependency, but not enough to accept the overall association as clinically meaningful under the stated threshold. I do not reject H15 because the two estimates are concordant and the intervals contain meaningful positive effects, but I close the overall H15 investigation because further same-data validation would not be as informative as testing whether the effect is diluted or enriched in a biologically relevant subtype. The registered adenocarcinoma-specific refinement is a conservative follow-up: ERBB2 signaling may be enriched in adenocarcinoma, so subtype restriction could reveal a larger clinically meaningful association. If that subgroup estimate remains near or below the 10% threshold and crosses zero, it would further argue that the ERBB2-STAT3 association is not robust at a meaningful magnitude. All conclusions remain dataset-specific associations, not causal claims or generalizable predictions.

The current priority is to turn the three large accepted dataset associations into more interpretable, robust, and specific findings rather than only adding new predictors. First, I registered direct estimates of the accepted effects in non-Avana CRISPR screens. We already accepted that the SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2, MSI-high/WRN, and KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 associations persist in the dominant Avana library and in higher-ROC screens. Testing the same contrasts in non-Avana libraries is an important orthogonal technical check: if the effects remain large and correctly signed there, they are less likely to be an artifact of the dominant library. Because the non-Avana subset is smaller, I kept these as direct comparisons with adequate expected cell counts rather than over-restricting by multiple quality filters. Second, I registered marker-null specificity interactions. The research markers D, E, and F are stated to have no assigned biological role, so a biologically credible dependency association should not be strongly modified by the corresponding marker. These interaction tests ask whether the accepted effects are diluted or concentrated in marker-positive lines. Near-zero interactions would increase confidence that the huge accepted effects are not driven by latent marker-positive structure; large marker interactions would be a warning about dataset-specific confounding and would need reconsideration. Third, I added two focused biological probes for under-tested predictor-outcome pairs. TP53 loss versus USP7 dependency is biologically motivated because USP7 participates in the MDM2-p53 axis, so TP53-deficient lines may depend less on USP7; I therefore registered a positive signed direction expecting weaker USP7 dependency in TP53-loss lines. BRAF V600E versus RIT1 dependency is plausible because RIT1 is a RAS/MAPK-adjacent GTPase and BRAF-mutant lines may use alternate MAPK-pathway dependencies; I registered a negative direction expecting stronger RIT1 dependency. All proposals are still discovery associations within the supplied lung-lineage dataset, not causal claims or external generalizability claims.

I request 12 new discovery analyses focused on the highest-value unresolved questions: technical robustness, biological subtype heterogeneity, marker-null specificity, and one follow-up of the borderline ERBB2–STAT3 result. No new evidence is available yet, so no assessments are changed. First, I test the three accepted large associations under high Cas9 activity (H30-H32), an orthogonal screen-quality metric not covered by the already accepted Avana-library and high screen_roc_auc restrictions. For signed directions, persistence should appear as large positive signed estimates. Second, I test library independence by estimating SMARCA4-loss and KEAP1-loss effects in non-Avana screens (H43, H45). I omit H44 for WRN because the expected MSI-high cell in non-Avana screens may be sparse: crispr_library_avana=0 has about 235 lines overall, and with MSI-high prevalence 6.5% the exposed cell is expected to be near 15, below the 20-observation requirement. WRN technical robustness is already covered by high screen_roc_auc and will be tested under high Cas9 activity. Third, I test subtype interaction (H25-H27) for adenocarcinoma versus non-adenocarcinoma; near-zero signed interactions would indicate that the accepted effects are not merely artifacts of the dominant adenocarcinoma subtype. Fourth, I test research-marker interaction effects (H46-H48); because these markers have no assigned biological role, large heterogeneity by marker positivity would be a specificity warning. Finally, I test the adenocarcinoma-specific ERBB2-amplification association with STAT3 dependency (H42). H15 was concordant but borderline: discovery +0.0222 and independent validation +0.0243, both below the approximate 0.028 absolute value corresponding to 10% for STAT3-scale outcomes. H42 tests whether the association is enriched in adenocarcinoma; a near-zero or wide interval crossing null would further support that the overall association is not clinically meaningful. All requested tests are discovery analyses in the supplied dataset with 95% Welch intervals and cell-count diagnostics.

The new results further strengthen the three large accepted dataset associations. In high-Cas9 screens, SMARCA4-loss versus dependency_SMARCA2 is +0.788 (CI +0.756 to +0.820), MSI-high versus dependency_WRN is +0.776 (CI +0.728 to +0.824), and KEAP1-loss versus dependency_NFE2L2 is +0.800 (CI +0.769 to +0.831). In non-Avana screens, SMARCA4-loss versus SMARCA2 is +0.801 (CI +0.748 to +0.853) and KEAP1-loss versus NFE2L2 is +0.794 (CI +0.746 to +0.842). These are not independent external validations, but they are informative same-dataset technical robustness checks: the huge signed effects remain far above clinical thresholds when dominant library or high Cas9 activity subsets are used. I accept and close these restricted robustness claims.

The adenocarcinoma interaction tests mostly do not show clinically meaningful modification of the accepted effects. H25 has signed estimate -0.028 (CI -0.076 to +0.020); the maximum positive claim-direction magnitude is below the approximate 0.041 threshold for a 10% effect on dependency_SMARCA2, so I reject it. H26 and H27 are near null (-0.021 and -0.012), and their intervals include some support above their approximate 0.030 absolute thresholds, so I do not reject them outright, but I close them because they are low-priority specificity checks and there is no clear evidence that adenocarcinoma subtype drives the accepted effects.

The research-marker interaction tests are reassuringly small: H46 +0.008, H47 -0.005, and H48 +0.007. However, their 95% intervals still include some marker-specific differences above a 10%-scale threshold, so I leave these interaction claims unresolved but closed as direct specificity evidence rather than continue validation. I registered a companion direct control for marker F against dependency_NFE2L2 because the existing interaction companion lacks the corresponding direct marker-outcome control.

H42, ERBB2 amplification versus dependency_STAT3 within adenocarcinoma, gives signed estimate +0.021 (CI -0.024 to +0.066). The point estimate is below the approximately 0.028 absolute threshold corresponding to a 10% effect for STAT3-scale outcomes, and the interval crosses null. This does not support clinically meaningful enrichment in adenocarcinoma. Since H15 overall was also borderline and already independently validated without reaching the threshold, I leave H42 unresolved but closed and do not request validation. I omitted a validation request because the huge accepted effects do not need it and the remaining borderline subgroup effect is unlikely to become interpretable with a wider independent interval. All conclusions remain associations within the supplied lung-lineage dataset, not causal claims or generalizable predictions.

The newly released independent validation for H24 is decisive. In high screen-quality screens, the KEAP1-loss association with weaker dependency_NFE2L2 has signed estimate +0.799 with independent 95% interval +0.759 to +0.839, using the stricter validation alpha. This is orders of magnitude larger than any plausible 10%-relative threshold for NFE2L2-scale outcomes and lies far from both the null and any meaningful opposite-direction effect. Thus H24 is accepted and closed: the KEAP1-loss effect is robust even when restricted to high-quality screens, and the independent validation interval supports the same huge positive signed association. Because this validates the high-ROC restricted contrast, I also close the broader accepted main effect H17; the original huge association remains accepted and now has supportive independent evidence, but further investigation of this main effect would be less informative than testing new predictors or specificity probes.

For the overdue response deadline on H3, the independent validation changes the conclusion from unresolved to reject. Discovery had signed estimate +0.0252 with interval -0.0003 to +0.0507, barely near the approximately 0.025 absolute threshold for a 10% effect on dependency_EGFR and still including null. Independent validation gave signed estimate -0.0060 with interval -0.0497 to +0.0377, i.e., a small opposite-direction point estimate and wide uncertainty. The combination does not support a clinically meaningful EGFR-amplification association with stronger dependency_EGFR. I therefore reject and close H3 and also close the adenocarcinoma refinement H35 as low priority, because the main EGFR-amplification effect is not supported.

The three major accepted dataset associations are now sufficiently characterized for the same dataset. SMARCA4-loss versus stronger dependency_SMARCA2 remains accepted, with huge direct estimates and robustness across Avana, non-Avana, high screen-quality, and high-Cas9 subsets. MSI-high versus stronger dependency_WRN remains accepted, with huge direct estimates and robustness across high ROC and high Cas9 subsets; the non-Avana WRN cell was expected sparse and is not needed for closure. KEAP1-loss versus weaker dependency_NFE2L2 remains accepted, with robustness across library, screen quality, Cas9 activity, non-Avana screens, and now independent validation of the high-ROC restricted estimate. I close the main accepted effects H6, H8, and H17 to focus future analysis on unresolved predictors and specificity probes rather than repeatedly validating effects that are already far above the clinical threshold.

I also close H33, the ARID1A-loss interaction modifying the SMARCA4-loss effect on dependency_SMARCA2, because the direct ARID1A-positive probe H39 is the better next test and the interaction estimate +0.037 was imprecise and near the SMARCA2-scale 10% threshold. The current best next set of discovery analyses is the active unrun probe set: EGFR amplification versus TMED10 dependency, TP53 loss versus RPL11 dependency, marker-null direct controls, PIK3CA mutation versus STAT3 dependency, SMARCA4-loss effect restricted to ARID1A-loss lines, KRAS and ERBB2 subtype probes, TP53 loss versus USP7 dependency, BRAF V600E versus RIT1 dependency, and marker F versus NFE2L2 dependency. All conclusions remain associations within the supplied lung-lineage CRISPR dataset, not causal claims or claims of external generalizability.

With the three large SMARCA2, WRN, and NFE2L2 associations now characterized and closed for practical purposes, the next step is to expand coverage toward biologically plausible predictor-outcome pairs and specificity controls. The strongest new candidates are mechanistically motivated synthetic-lethality or pathway dependencies. For dependency_TMED10, ER-Golgi trafficking can support receptor tyrosine kinase and secretory signaling; ERBB2-amplified lines may therefore show stronger TMED10 dependency, so I registered a negative direction. For dependency_WRN, I registered BRCA2 loss as an independent probe of DNA repair/replication stress synthetic lethality, restricted to MSI-negative lines to test whether a WRN association can exist apart from the accepted MSI-high effect. For dependency_NFE2L2, I registered the accepted KEAP1-loss effect within STK11-loss lines, a clinically relevant co-mutation context in lung adenocarcinoma, using the same weaker-dependency direction as the accepted KEAP1 association. MYC amplification is a broad proliferative and transcriptional driver, so I registered MYC amplification against dependency_STAT3 and dependency_KIF18A to test whether amplified MYC contexts depend more on STAT3 transcriptional programs or mitotic machinery. Cross-RTK relationships are also worth probing: EGFR-amplified lines may depend more on ERBB2 through receptor network coactivation, so I registered ERBB2 dependency against EGFR amplification. Similarly, KRAS-mutant lines may bypass BRAF, giving a weaker BRAF dependency, and EGFR-amplified lines might exploit RIT1-related RAS/MAPK signaling; these are more exploratory but cell counts are adequate. CDKN2A loss is registered against MDM2 dependency because the CDKN2A locus includes p14ARF, an upstream regulator of the MDM2-p53 axis, though the direction is biologically complex and remains uncertain. Finally, I added direct marker-null controls for WRN and NFE2L2 using markers D, E, and F. These markers have no assigned biological role; near-zero associations would support that the large accepted effects are not driven by latent marker-defined structure, whereas substantial marker associations would caution against interpreting the accepted effects as specific to the intended biological predictors. All proposals are associations within the supplied lung-lineage dataset, not causal claims or claims of external generalizability.

No assessments are due in this stage. I request 12 discovery analyses that maximize scientific value across predictor-outcome coverage, mechanistic plausibility, and specificity. The selected set tests: (1) EGFR- and ERBB2-amplification effects on dependency_TMED10 for ER-Golgi trafficking/RTK signaling hypotheses; (2) TP53-loss effects on dependency_RPL11 and dependency_USP7, and CDKN2A-loss effects on dependency_MDM2, as probes of the p53/ARF/ribosome-stress axis; (3) BRCA2 loss versus dependency_WRN in MSI-high-negative lines, testing whether a WRN association can exist independently of the accepted MSI-high effect; (4) the accepted KEAP1-loss effect on dependency_NFE2L2 within STK11-loss lines, testing persistence in a clinically relevant co-mutation context; (5) cross-pathway RTK/MAPK probes EGFR amplification versus dependency_ERBB2 and KRAS mutation versus dependency_BRAF; (6) PIK3CA mutation versus dependency_STAT3 and MYC amplification versus dependency_KIF18A as broader proliferative/signaling probes; and (7) a direct marker-null control, marker F versus dependency_NFE2L2, to check that the accepted KEAP1-NFE2L2 signal is not accompanied by a strong association with an assay lacking assigned biology. These are discovery tests with 95% Welch intervals and cell-count diagnostics; any effect-size judgments will be made in appraise using outcome-scale 10% thresholds and uncertainty.

The new discovery batch adds one very large new association, one clearly meaningful moderate association, and several mostly null or imprecise probes. H49, TP53 loss versus dependency_USP7, has signed estimate +0.802 (CI +0.782 to +0.822), which is far beyond any plausible 10% clinical threshold for USP7-scale outcomes and also far beyond null. I accept this as a strong same-dataset association and keep it active while requesting independent validation because it is a new large finding and independent confirmation would be scientifically valuable. H54, the accepted KEAP1-loss association restricted to STK11-loss lines, has signed estimate +0.775 (CI +0.727 to +0.823), supporting persistence of the large weaker-NFE2L2 effect in this co-mutation context; because the main KEAP1 effect is already accepted and heavily checked, this robustness claim is accepted and closed. H59, CDKN2A loss versus dependency_MDM2, has signed estimate +0.117 (CI +0.082 to +0.152); the lower bound exceeds the approximate 0.026 absolute 10% threshold for MDM2-scale outcomes, so I accept it as a meaningful dataset association and keep it active for future technical and specificity checks. H16 is clinically insignificant for the TP53-loss direction on RPL11: signed estimate +0.004 with upper bound +0.024 below the approximate 0.025 RPL11 threshold, so I reject it. H57, H58, and H37 are signed negative or near-null; their positive claim-direction upper bounds are well below outcome-scale 10% thresholds, so the hypothesized directions are rejected, even though the intervals may allow some opposite-direction signal. H14, H52, H53, and H56 are near-null but their intervals include values around or slightly above the relevant 10% thresholds, so I leave them unresolved but closed as low-yield follow-up checks. H51 is a marker-null direct control for marker F and dependency_NFE2L2; it is reassuringly near-null, but the interval still permits marginal positive and negative differences, so it remains unresolved and closed as specificity evidence. I did not request validation for the huge accepted H54, nor for the rejected or low-yield unresolved claims. I registered same-dataset technical robustness, marker-null, and one TP53 interaction proposal for the newly accepted H49 and H59 effects. All conclusions remain associations in the supplied lung-lineage dataset, not causal or generalizable claims.

The independent validation for H49 confirms the newly discovered TP53-loss association with dependency_USP7 and does so at a very large effect size. The discovery signed estimate was +0.802 (95% CI +0.782 to +0.822), and the independent validation signed estimate was +0.800 (strict independent interval +0.769 to +0.831). Because the signed direction is positive and dependency scores are more negative when stronger, this means TP53 loss is associated with much weaker USP7 dependency. The validation interval is far above any plausible 10% clinical-threshold magnitude on the USP7 scale and far from null, so I accept H49 as a robust same-dataset association and close further investigation of the main effect. This gives a fourth major accepted main association alongside SMARCA4-loss -> stronger SMARCA2 dependency, MSI-high -> stronger WRN dependency, and KEAP1-loss -> weaker NFE2L2 dependency. The accepted CDKN2A-loss -> stronger MDM2 association (H59) remains active mainly for technical robustness and biological-context probes.

For H15, the response deadline on the ERBB2-amplification -> dependency_STAT3 claim is now met by independent validation. The discovery signed estimate was +0.0222 (CI -0.0147 to +0.0592), and the validation signed estimate was +0.0243 (independent interval -0.0291 to +0.0776). For dependency_STAT3, whose observed mean is about -0.282, a 10% relative difference corresponds roughly to an absolute signed effect around +0.028 in the proposed direction. Both point estimates are below that threshold, and the validation interval includes null as well as a small opposite-direction effect. Therefore the validation does not rescue the borderline discovery signal. I do not accept the claim of a clinically meaningful ERBB2-amplification association with stronger STAT3 dependency. I leave it unresolved because the upper validation interval still permits a clinically meaningful positive difference, but I keep it closed because it is low priority and the combined evidence suggests a small or uncertain effect rather than a clear large one.

The current supported dataset-level findings are: SMARCA4 loss is associated with stronger SMARCA2 dependency; MSI-high is associated with stronger WRN dependency; KEAP1 loss is associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency, including in STK11-loss lines and under independent validation of the high-quality-screen subset; TP53 loss is associated with weaker USP7 dependency; and CDKN2A loss is associated with stronger MDM2 dependency, supported by a discovery lower bound clearly above the approximate MDM2 10% threshold. These are associations within the supplied lung-lineage CRISPR dataset, not causal claims and not claims of external generalizability. The next most informative analyses are context and specificity probes for the newly accepted H49 and H59 effects: non-Avana screen robustness, TP53-status stratification of the CDKN2A-MDM2 effect, and marker-null controls. If those remain reassuring, future work can return to the remaining active subtype, MAPK, and ARID1A/SMARCA2 probes.

The dataset now supports five major same-dataset associations: SMARCA4 loss is associated with stronger dependency_SMARCA2, MSI-high with stronger dependency_WRN, KEAP1 loss with weaker dependency_NFE2L2, TP53 loss with weaker dependency_USP7 after independent validation, and CDKN2A loss with stronger dependency_MDM2. The main effect of each accepted association has already been checked extensively, so the next scientifically useful work is specificity testing, co-deletion/context testing, and broadening coverage to less tested predictor-outcome pairs.

For the newly accepted CDKN2A-loss association with stronger dependency_MDM2, MTAP loss is an important co-deletion probe because MTAP is frequently co-deleted with CDKN2A. A strong MTAP-loss association would suggest that the MDM2 signal may reflect broader 9p21 deletion or linked genomic structure, whereas a near-null MTAP result would increase confidence that the association is more specific to CDKN2A loss or its regulatory products. I also registered missing marker-null direct controls for the newly accepted MDM2 and USP7 effects, for SMARCA2, and as part of the marker-specificity program. Markers D, E, and F have no assigned biology; near-zero associations would argue against the large accepted effects being driven by latent marker-defined structure, whereas substantial marker associations would caution against over-specific biological interpretation.

For SWI/SNF biology, I registered a direct ARID1A-loss versus dependency_SMARCA2 contrast. The accepted SMARCA4-loss effect is very large, but a direct ARID1A-loss effect would test whether the dependency is a broader SWI/SNF complex feature or more specific to SMARCA4 loss. I also registered SMARCA4 loss versus dependency_POLR2A to test a transcriptional dependency hypothesis: chromatin-remodeler loss may alter RNA polymerase II dependency. RB1 loss versus dependency_DHX9 tests whether replication/transcription stress associated with RB1 loss increases dependence on an RNA helicase resolving R loops. NF1 loss versus dependency_BRAF tests RAS/MAPK bypass: if NF1 loss activates upstream signaling, BRAF could become less essential, though the direction remains biologically contestable. STK11 loss versus dependency_NFE2L2, restricted to KEAP1 wild-type lines, tests whether STK11 loss has an independent association with NRF2-pathway dependency rather than merely reflecting co-occurring KEAP1 loss. Finally, ERBB2 amplification versus dependency_EGFR and a high-Cas9 refinement of RB1 loss versus dependency_KIF18A broaden coverage of RTK coactivation and a borderline mitotic dependency signal. All of these remain associations within the supplied lung-lineage CRISPR dataset, not causal or generalizable claims.

No assessments are due in this stage. I request 12 discovery analyses that balance mechanistic specificity, technical/contextual robustness, and broader predictor-outcome coverage.

For the newly accepted CDKN2A-loss association with stronger dependency_MDM2, I test: MTAP co-deletion (H78) to assess whether the MDM2 signal is attributable specifically to CDKN2A loss or to broader 9p21 deletion; CDKN2A-loss effects stratified by TP53 status (H75 and H76) to test independence from TP53 loss and interpret potential p14ARF-p53-MDM2 pathway structure; and non-Avana library robustness (H74) to address technical heterogeneity. Marker D direct control on dependency_MDM2 (H80) tests whether latent marker-defined structure can mimic the CDKN2A-MDM2 association.

For the accepted TP53-loss/USP7 association, I request marker D control (H77) as a negative-control specificity check for the newly validated USP7 signal.

For SWI/SNF biology, H83 directly tests ARID1A loss versus dependency_SMARCA2, whereas H85 tests whether SMARCA4 loss also affects dependency_POLR2A. These complement the accepted SMARCA4-SMARCA2 association by testing broader complex dependence and transcriptional dependency.

The remaining selected analyses broaden coverage with biologically motivated probes: RB1 loss versus dependency_DHX9 (H84) tests replication/transcription-stress dependence; NF1 loss versus dependency_BRAF (H86) tests RAS/MAPK bypass and weakened BRAF dependency; STK11 loss versus dependency_NFE2L2 within KEAP1 wild-type lines (H87) tests whether STK11 loss has an association apart from KEAP1; and RB1 loss versus dependency_KIF18A under high Cas9 activity (H88) refines a borderline mitotic signal. All selected claims are new evidence requests and are interpreted as associations within the supplied dataset, not causal or generalizable claims.

The new batch primarily strengthens the accepted CDKN2A-loss association with stronger MDM2 dependency and gives one unexpected RB1-DHX9 signal in the opposite direction to the registered hypothesis.

For MDM2 specificity and robustness, H75 shows CDKN2A loss in TP53-loss-negative lines with signed estimate +0.119 (95% CI +0.079 to +0.158), and H76 shows CDKN2A loss in TP53-loss lines with signed estimate +0.111 (95% CI +0.035 to +0.186). Both lower bounds exceed the approximate absolute 10% MDM2 threshold (~0.027), so the association is accepted in both TP53 strata. H74 in non-Avana screens gives +0.125 (95% CI +0.029 to +0.222), also above threshold, although with small cells and wider uncertainty. Together with H59, these results make broader technical or TP53-status explanations less plausible, though the non-Avana estimate is imprecise and should not be overinterpreted.

MTAP co-deletion is not near enough to explain the CDKN2A effect to warrant further priority follow-up: H78 has signed estimate +0.019 (95% CI -0.008 to +0.045), far smaller than the CDKN2A effect but still permitting a clinically meaningful MTAP association. I mark it unresolved but closed. Marker controls are also reassuringly small: H80 for marker D on MDM2 gives +0.019 (95% CI -0.001 to +0.039), and H77 for marker D on USP7 gives +0.005 (95% CI -0.027 to +0.038). These do not support the large accepted effects being driven by marker-defined latent structure, but because the intervals still include threshold-scale effects, I keep them unresolved and closed as specificity evidence rather than accept a strict null.

For other probes, H83 ARID1A loss versus dependency_SMARCA2 fails the proposed stronger-dependency direction: signed estimate -0.017 with upper bound +0.023, below the SMARCA2 threshold (~0.042). I reject that original claim, while noting a possible opposite-direction signal. H85 SMARCA4 loss versus dependency_POLR2A also fails its proposed direction: upper bound +0.014 below the POLR2A threshold (~0.026), so I reject it as low-yield. H84 RB1 loss versus dependency_DHX9 was registered for stronger DHX9 dependency, but the signed interval is entirely negative (-0.061 to -0.009), with magnitude exceeding the DHX9 threshold (~0.025) in the opposite direction, suggesting RB1 loss is associated with weaker DHX9 dependency. I reject the original claim and register a reversal for later analysis.

H86 NF1 loss versus dependency_BRAF remains a biologically plausible borderline positive signal: +0.021 (95% CI -0.005 to +0.047), around the BRAF threshold (~0.025). I leave it active because validation or future context work may clarify it. H87 STK11 loss versus dependency_NFE2L2 in KEAP1-wild-type lines is near-null and does not support an independent STK11 effect in the proposed direction; because the interval still allows small threshold-scale effects, I mark it unresolved but closed. H88 high-Cas9 RB1 loss versus dependency_KIF18A is imprecise and opposite to the proposed direction; I close it as low-yield.

I request independent validation for H59, the main CDKN2A-loss versus dependency_MDM2 association, because it is a new accepted meaningful effect and independent confirmation is more valuable now than validating a borderline secondary context. All conclusions remain associations in this supplied lung-lineage dataset.

The two due validation items strengthen the current core findings. For H24, KEAP1 loss in high-quality screens versus dependency_NFE2L2, the high-quality discovery signed estimate was +0.790 (95% CI +0.763 to +0.816), and the strict independent validation signed estimate was +0.799 (independent interval +0.759 to +0.839). Because the direction is positive on a negative-valued dependency score, this corresponds to much weaker NFE2L2 dependency in KEAP1-loss lines. The independent interval is extremely far from null and far above any plausible 10% clinical threshold on the NFE2L2 scale, so H24 remains accepted and is closed. This reinforces the broader accepted KEAP1-loss association while remaining limited to the supplied lung-lineage CRISPR dataset.

For H59, CDKN2A loss versus dependency_MDM2, the discovery signed estimate was +0.117 (95% CI +0.082 to +0.152), and the independent validation signed estimate was +0.116 (independent interval +0.065 to +0.166). For dependency_MDM2, whose absolute scale is roughly near -0.27, the approximate 10% clinical threshold is about 0.027 in signed magnitude. Both discovery and validation lower bounds exceed that threshold, and the intervals are consistent. Since this claim direction is negative on the raw score, the accepted interpretation is that CDKN2A-loss lines have more negative MDM2 dependency scores, i.e. stronger MDM2 dependency. I therefore accept H59, close the main effect, and retain it as one of the main same-dataset associations.

The supported dataset-level core associations are now: SMARCA4 loss is associated with stronger SMARCA2 dependency; MSI-high is associated with stronger WRN dependency; KEAP1 loss is associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency, with robust support in high-quality and other technical contexts and independent validation of the high-quality subset; TP53 loss is associated with weaker USP7 dependency, independently validated; and CDKN2A loss is associated with stronger MDM2 dependency, independently validated. These are associations within this dataset, not causal claims and not claims of external generalizability.

The most informative next unresolved signal is H90, the reversal of H84. RB1 loss was not associated with stronger DHX9 dependency as originally hypothesized; instead, the reversal shows a positive signed raw difference of +0.0348 (95% CI +0.0091 to +0.0605), suggesting weaker DHX9 dependency in RB1-loss lines. The point estimate exceeds the approximate 0.025 DHX9 threshold, but the lower bound is below threshold and uncertainty is nontrivial, so I keep H90 active for same-dataset robustness and likely validation. H86, NF1 loss versus weaker BRAF dependency, remains borderline: +0.0211 with interval -0.0046 to +0.0468, around but not clearly above the approximate 0.025 BRAF threshold. It remains active but lower priority than H90.

Several probes produced negative or low-yield results. ARID1A loss did not support the hypothesized stronger SMARCA2 dependency, and SMARCA4 loss did not support a stronger POLR2A dependency in the registered direction. MTAP co-deletion was much smaller than the CDKN2A effect, and marker controls were near-null relative to the accepted large effects, though they do not strictly exclude small clinically meaningful marker associations. I defer most remaining active marker-null, technical robustness, subtype, and RTK probes because they are less informative than completing validation/robustness for the newly emerging RB1-DHX9 reversal and clarifying NF1-BRAF. The next analyses should focus on whether H90 and H86 survive screen-library, Cas9-activity, and screen-quality restrictions, with H90 as the primary validation candidate.

The five core same-dataset associations are now stable: SMARCA4 loss with stronger SMARCA2 dependency, MSI-high with stronger WRN dependency, KEAP1 loss with weaker NFE2L2 dependency, TP53 loss with weaker USP7 dependency, and CDKN2A loss with stronger MDM2 dependency. The most informative active unresolved signals are the RB1-loss reversal for dependency_DHX9 and the borderline NF1-loss signal for dependency_BRAF. For RB1 loss, the existing signed estimate (+0.0348; CI +0.009 to +0.061) exceeds the approximate 10% DHX9 threshold (~0.025), but the lower bound remains near threshold, so context-specific and specificity probes are useful before considering validation. I therefore registered RB1-loss versus dependency_DHX9 separately in TP53-loss and TP53-loss-negative lines. A positive difference in both strata would support a general RB1-DHX9 association; a positive difference only in one stratum would suggest TP53-context specificity; and a null result would reduce priority. I also registered research-marker-D null controls for the emerging DHX9 signal and for the borderline BRAF signal. These constructed markers have no assigned biology; near-zero estimates would argue against latent marker-defined structure producing these apparent gene-dependency differences, whereas substantial marker associations would caution against overly specific interpretation.

I also broaden coverage with mechanistically motivated MAPK and STAT3 probes. NF1 loss and BRAF V600E are expected, if plausible, to weaken dependency_KRAS because both can increase downstream MAPK signaling or bypass upstream KRAS requirement, though stronger KRAS dependency or no effect remain alternatives. STK11 loss and PTEN loss are hypothesized to increase STAT3 dependency because LKB1 loss and PI3K/AKT-related pathway alteration can activate stress, metabolic, or cytokine/STAT3-associated programs, though these remain exploratory associations only. Thresholds are approximate relative 10% scales based on absolute mean dependency values: DHX9/BRAF/KRAS roughly 0.025 and STAT3 roughly 0.028. All proposed conclusions are limited to the supplied lung-lineage CRISPR dataset, not causal or generalizable claims.

No assessments are due, and I request 12 previously registered untested discovery analyses. These analyses balance focused follow-up on the most informative unresolved signals with broader mechanistic coverage.

The primary priority is H90, the reversal of H84: RB1 loss was associated with weaker DHX9 dependency in the overall lung-lineage dataset (signed estimate +0.0348; 95% CI +0.0091 to +0.0605). Because the point estimate is above the approximate 10% clinical threshold on the DHX9 absolute-scale (~0.025) but the lower bound is below threshold, the signal is plausible but not yet robust enough to accept. The requested analyses test whether this signal persists in higher-quality or more homogeneous technical contexts and whether it is specific to RB1 loss rather than a byproduct of TP53 co-alteration or latent marker-defined structure. H91 tests Avana-library screens; H92 tests high-Cas9 screens; H93 tests high screen-quality screens. H96 and H97 stratify by TP53 loss to test whether the RB1-DHX9 association occurs independently of TP53 status. H98 is a marker-D null control for dependency_DHX9: because marker D has no assigned biology, a large marker-D association would caution that the apparent RB1-DHX9 signal may reflect non-specific latent assay structure, whereas a near-null marker-D contrast would increase confidence that the RB1 association is not a generic marker artifact.

The secondary priority is H86, NF1 loss versus weaker BRAF dependency. The overall estimate is borderline (signed estimate +0.0211; 95% CI -0.0046 to +0.0468), near the approximate BRAF threshold (~0.025) but not clearly above threshold. H94 tests Avana-library screens, H95 tests high-Cas9 screens, and H99 provides a marker-D null control for dependency_BRAF. If the NF1-BRAF association weakens in stringent subsets or marker-D shows a similarly large effect, the claim should be de-prioritized. If it persists and marker-D remains near-null, it may merit later validation.

I also use the remaining slots for biologically motivated broad exploration. H100 tests whether NF1 loss is associated with weaker KRAS dependency, reflecting possible MAPK-pathway bypass or reduced reliance on upstream KRAS signaling. H101 tests whether BRAF V600E is associated with weaker KRAS dependency, a related downstream MAPK bypass hypothesis. H102 tests STK11 loss versus stronger STAT3 dependency, motivated by LKB1/mTOR/AMPK-related stress signaling and possible STAT3 involvement. All requested estimates will come from Welch independent-cell comparisons with 95% intervals and cell-size diagnostics; conclusions remain limited to associations within the supplied lung-lineage CRISPR dataset, not causality or external generalizability.

I defer H103, PTEN loss versus dependency_STAT3, because it is similar in pathway focus to H102 but less immediately complementary to the active MAPK and specificity work. The H90 validation decision will primarily depend on whether H91, H92, H93, H96, and H97 maintain positive estimates with bounds near or above threshold, and whether H98 is near-null.

I audited the new evidence as critical reviewer. The RB1-loss and dependency_DHX9 signal remains the most informative unresolved claim, but these new analyses are mostly subset or marker-control tests and do not by themselves establish a clinically robust effect. H91 in Avana-library screens gives +0.0389 (95% CI +0.0126 to +0.0653), and H92 in high-Cas9 screens gives +0.0524 (+0.0159 to +0.0890). Because these are direction +1, positive values indicate weaker DHX9 dependency in RB1-loss lines. The intervals exclude null and are supportive, but their lower bounds remain below the approximate 10% DHX9 scale (~0.025), so I keep them unresolved. H93 in high screen-quality screens gives +0.0192 (-0.0121 to +0.0506), which is below threshold and imprecise; this does not reject the effect but weakens the claim of general robustness, so I defer it rather than prioritize further same-dataset subset work. TP53 stratification is informative: H96 gives +0.0513 (+0.0022 to +0.1004) in TP53-loss lines and H97 gives +0.0288 (-0.0013 to +0.0589) in TP53-loss-negative lines. Both are positive, arguing against a purely TP53-co-loss explanation, but both are wide and not convincingly above the clinical threshold. H98 marker-D control for DHX9 gives -0.0102 (-0.0261 to +0.0057), far below a clinically meaningful positive marker-D effect, so I reject the registered positive marker-D DHX9 association and close it as a specificity check. However, marker controls do not rule out confounding by measured or unmeasured co-alterations, and marker D's near-null result is only weak specificity evidence because a single arbitrary binary marker cannot exclude latent structure. Given that H90/H91/H92 are consistent positives, H93 is not, and marker controls are near-null, independent validation of H90 is the most useful next step. I request validation for H90. If validation has a lower bound near or above the approximate 0.025 DHX9 scale, accept H90; if it fails or is below threshold, close or defer the RB1-DHX9 family. The NF1-BRAF secondary claim is not improved by new evidence: H94 is +0.0198 (-0.0068 to +0.0464), H95 is -0.0032 (-0.0451 to +0.0388), and marker-D BRAF control H99 is -0.0028 (-0.0186 to +0.0130). I close H94 and H95 as low-yield and defer the parent H86. Broad MAPK KRAS probes H100/H101 and STAT3 probe H102 are borderline or below threshold and imprecise; I defer them behind H90 validation. All interpretations remain associations in this supplied lung-lineage CRISPR dataset, not causal or generalizable claims.

The newly delivered validation responses materially change the current conclusions. First, H49 was already an accepted discovery association: TP53-loss lines had higher, less-negative dependency_USP7 scores than TP53-loss-negative lines, interpreted as weaker USP7 dependency. The independent validation estimate is very consistent with discovery: signed validation estimate +0.800 with independent interval +0.769 to +0.831, compared with discovery +0.802, +0.782 to +0.822. This effect is extremely large relative to any approximate 10% clinical-scale threshold for dependency_USP7 and the validation interval remains far from both null and threshold-scale null. I therefore accept H49 and close it as a supported same-dataset association, with no causal or external generalizability claim.

Second, H36, MYC amplification versus dependency_RPL11, was already rejected on discovery evidence because the registered stronger-dependency direction was not supported by the discovery interval. The independent validation does not rescue the claim: the signed validation estimate is small, +0.015, with independent interval -0.015 to +0.044. For the registered direction, this is not a clinically meaningful robust effect, and the validation is inconsistent with the discovery direction. I keep H36 rejected and closed as a negative/low-yield probe.

Third, H90, the reversal of H84 for RB1 loss versus dependency_DHX9, was the key unresolved signal. H90 claimed that RB1-loss lines have weaker DHX9 dependency, i.e. higher and less-negative dependency_DHX9 scores. Discovery gave a suggestive positive signed estimate +0.0348, interval +0.0091 to +0.0605. The point estimate exceeded the approximate 10% DHX9 threshold (~0.025), but the lower bound was below threshold, motivating independent validation. The independent validation estimate is -0.0069, independent interval -0.0446 to +0.0309. Thus the validation point estimate is near zero and opposite to the claim, and the interval includes null, clinically meaningful positive effects, and clinically meaningful negative effects. Taken as a whole, the overall RB1-loss/DHX9 association is not supported as scientifically meaningful: discovery was borderline, the strict subset evidence was heterogeneous, and independent validation failed. I therefore reject H90 and close the investigation. The related same-dataset subset claims H91, H92, H93, H96, and H97 remain unresolved as exploratory subset estimates but are closed from active follow-up because they no longer provide a robust route to an accepted overall association.

The supported core same-dataset associations remain: SMARCA4 loss is associated with stronger SMARCA2 dependency; MSI-high is associated with stronger WRN dependency; KEAP1 loss is associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency, with independent validation in the high-screen-quality subset; TP53 loss is associated with weaker USP7 dependency, now independently validated; and CDKN2A loss is associated with stronger MDM2 dependency, independently validated. Negative or low-yield results include the overall RB1-DHX9 reversal, MYC-amplification versus dependency_RPL11, ARID1A-loss versus dependency_SMARCA2 in the registered direction, SMARCA4-loss versus dependency_POLR2A in the registered direction, and marker-D positive associations used as specificity controls. The NF1-loss versus BRAF claim is closed as unresolved low-yield after borderline discovery and non-supportive robustness checks.

The most informative next analysis is the already registered but untested PTEN-loss versus dependency_STAT3 comparison. STAT3 has had only weak or borderline probes so far, and PTEN loss provides a mechanistically distinct PI3K/AKT/mTOR-related perturbation that could test whether STAT3 dependency is context-dependent in this dataset. If PTEN loss yields a discovery effect clearly above the approximate STAT3 clinical scale and with interval bounds supportive of clinical significance, I would consider accepting it without validation or requesting validation if the interval remains near threshold. If it is null or inconsistent, I would close the STAT3 pathway family and return to broader coverage of less-tested predictors and outcomes. All conclusions remain limited to associations in this supplied lung-lineage CRISPR dataset, not causal mechanisms or generalizable biology.
